question: The Spanish Government has announced that it will use some of the Recovery and Resilience Facility loans to buy debt securities issued by companies and direct equity stakes in companies. It has also announced that it will set up a new public company, which will bring together the state’s shareholdings in tech companies and finance its Telefónica share buy-up.

This means that up to EUR 40 billion will be invested through the Instituto de Crédito Oficial (Corporate State-Owned Entity, ICO) to ensure that members of the government sit on the boards of strategic private firms. In view of this: 1.

The Recovery and Resilience Facility was set up to boost economic recovery through reforms and investments that help make our companies more competitive. If national governments set up public companies and buy up shareholdings in private companies, is it more difficult to attract investments, and consolidate and expand companies?
Were the European recovery funds set up to finance protectionist policies and support for public companies, thereby undermining the competitiveness of private firms?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.7.2024) As per Article 17 of the Regulation, the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) can support public investment and public schemes that aim to incentivise private investments. This can be done through grant or subsidy schemes, or through financial instruments such as loans, guarantees or equity participations.

Such investments have the capacity to crowd-in additional private investments, provided they target clearly identified market failures linked with the objectives of the RRF. In the case of Spain, the Instituto de Crédito Official is one of the key implementing partners for such measures which were included with Spain’s request for additional loans in 2023.

There are prescriptive conditions included in the Annex to the Council’s Implementing Decision to these measures which take the following form: ‘The final investment decision of the Facility shall be taken by an investment committee or other relevant equivalent governing body and approved by a majority of votes from members who are independent from the Spanish Government.

For intermediated investments, the final investment decision shall be taken by the intermediaries’. These provisions have been included for a broad range of measures where the Instituto de Crédito Oficial (Corporate State-Owned Entity, ICO) is the implementing partner such as, inter alia, C2.I7, C13.I6 and C13.I7. In line with Art. 17.

1 of the RRF Regulation, public schemes can be set up to incentivise private investment and improve access to finance to companies. State aid rules fully apply to the measures funded by the RRF. Therefore, Member States should ensure that all investments, including implemented via financial instruments, comply with the relevant EU State aid rules and follow all State aid procedures.
